extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: General critical guidance on judging poets, poetic style, and the proper conduct of authors and critics; addresses qualities of genius vs. talent, common stylistic vices, and what constitutes fair criticism. Useful for writers and critics reflecting on standards of poetic merit and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risu honesto — the three sins of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Three faults likely to beset a young writer: (1) doleful egotism and recurrence of favourite phrases, with the double defect of being at once trite and licentious; (2) low creeping language and thoughts under the pretence of simplicity; (3) the indiscriminate use of elaborate and swelling language and imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge cites three sonnets he wrote to expose these vices; they are common characteristic faults of style in youthful writers and should be avoided. (Original examples and discussion given in the text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid laborious and florid diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Laborious and florid diction is of inferior worth and is a fault the author once practiced and later abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice should conform to better judgment; early florid manner may leave remnant faults but should be reformed toward naturalness and clarity (examples: the author's earlier blank verse and tragic passages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reforms must not be carried to excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Every reform, however necessary, will by weak minds be carried to an excess, which will itself need reforming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overcorrection when trying to remedy stylistic faults — swinging from one extreme (e.g. floridness) to another (affected simplicity) creates new problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irritability is not proof of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The common sarcasm genus irritabile vatum (the irritable tribe of poets) is unjustified; the greatest geniuses often exhibited calmness and self-possession rather than quarrelsomeness or personal irritability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attribute anger or testiness to genius; such traits more often derive from debility, superstition, fanaticism, bodily constitution, ill-health, or vanity. Coleridge cites Chaucer, Shakespeare, Spenser, and Milton as examples of serene temperaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate talent from genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Talent is the faculty of appropriating and applying the knowledge of others; genius is the creative and self-sufficing power that generates original conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In advanced literary stages, high talent plus taste may acquire the name of greatness, but true genius is identified by originality and the power to realize preconceptions independently — evaluate writers accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius shows sensibility to ideas over self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensibility, both quick and deep, is a component of genius, but a mark of true genius is that its sensibility is excited more by ideas, thoughts, and the ideal world than by personal interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect men of genius to live largely in the ideal; reduced preoccupation with their personal reputation or material interests is a sign of inward creative life, not indifference or lack of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish works of genius from manufactured literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine works of genius differ fundamentally from mechanically produced 'manufactured' literature; the latter is likened to a barrel-organ supplying both instrument and tune, and requires the least talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unconnected, epigrammatic, or mechanized stylistic tricks that spare the reader the trouble of thinking. The difference in kind is compared to that between an egg and an egg-shell — at a distance they may look alike, but are essentially different in substance and value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works should reward careful examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of polite literature are commonly perused with little examination by most readers, even able ones, until prompted; thus superficial devices may succeed briefly but do not substitute for depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose so that attentive readers are rewarded; do not rely on mere superficial cleverness that 'prevents vacancy while it indulges indolence' in the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism must focus on characteristic qualities, not accidental failures
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to decide the merits of a poet by accidental failures or individual faulty passages; where there is genius, defects point to characteristic beauties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the common critical anti-pattern of selecting and reprinting the worst passages from a volume to generalize about an author's merit; such practice is misleading and impudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose pretensions in durable, answerable forms, not irrecoverable conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: If one opposes the pretensions of individuals, do so in books which can be weighed and answered, rather than in ephemeral or irrecoverable conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present full reasons, limits, and modifications in written form so they can be properly examined and rebutted — avoid casual disputes that invite misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors have a right to protect their intellectual products
rubrics_metrics.description: The products of a writer's intellect and industry have claims to protection and to the author's interest and qualified anxiety regarding their reception and profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudence and fairness counsel authors to defend their works and to take due interest in their maintenance, especially when their livelihood or serious intentions are implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews and criticism significantly shape public reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical notices, anonymous or otherwise, constitute a large portion of an author's publicity and may familiarize readers with a name irrespective of whether mention was for praise or censure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that repeated critical exposure (positive or negative) builds reputation; Coleridge estimates critics have contributed to two-thirds of his own reputation. This is a pragmatic factor in how works are received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of reviewers who flatter the unworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: The eulogies of critics without taste or judgment are the natural reward of authors without feeling or genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for social and institutional conditions affecting critical taste; do not equate critical praise with intrinsic merit, especially when it originates from uninformed or fashionable sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider historical shifts in audience and critical authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation between authors and readers has changed: from books as oracles to instructive friends to entertaining companions, and now to a multitudinous public that claims critical authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or composing literature, take into account the current social shape of readership and criticism — understand that contemporary critical customs and popular expectations influence how works are received.
